questions.question: If some spiders build no webs, what do they use their silk for instead?

passages.quote: All spiders produce silk, although some spiders do not make webs.
Spiders such as the Salticidae venture from shelter and leave a trail of silk, use that as an emergency line in case of falling from inverted or vertical surfaces.

questions.question: If the role of male-spun silk in mating has barely been studied, how do we know silk is tied to courtship at all?

passages.quote: The function of male-produced silk in mating has received little study.[3]

questions.question: If Kevlar is stronger than spider silk, why is silk still held up as the superior material?

passages.quote: This enables a silk fibre to absorb a large amount of energy before breaking (toughness, the area under a stress-strain curve).
Weight for weight, silk is stronger than steel, but not as strong as Kevlar. Spider silk is, however, tougher than both.

questions.question: Why does pulling silk on demand rather than growing it continuously make artificial synthesis so hard to replicate?

passages.quote: It is pulled on demand from a precursor out of specialised glands,[41] rather than continuously grown like plant cell walls.[26]
Few strategies have produced silk that can efficiently be synthesised into fibres.

questions.question: What is the silk gland's valve actually thought to do, given that its purpose is still debated?

passages.quote: Though discovered some time ago, its precise purpose is still under discussion.

It is believed to assist in restarting and rejoining broken fibres,[61] acting much in the way of a helical pump, regulating the thickness of the fibre,[42] and/or clamping the fibre as a spider falls upon it.[61][62]

questions.question: If artificial silk only reaches half the strength and flexibility of natural silk, how can some synthetic spidroins be said to fully replicate its performance?

passages.quote: Fibers spun from these synthetic spidroins are the first to fully replicate the mechanical performance of natural spider silk by all common metrics.
Artificial spider silks have fewer and simpler proteins than natural dragline silk, and consequently offer half the diameter, strength, and flexibility of natural dragline silk.
